transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood), Jordan Patel (Redwood), Lena Ortiz (Redwood Marketing), Samir Rao (Redwood Audio), Sofia Martinez (Lumina), Dr. Rajiv Gupta (Lumina), Maya Lee (Lumina Marketing), Ethan Park (Lumina ML)

[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everybody, welcome to the Redwood customer spotlight. I'm Avery, product lead here at Redwood, and today we're talking with Lumina Health about their journey running LLMs in production. Hey, Sofia, Rajiv, Maya, Ethan, thanks for joining.

[00:32] Sofia (Lumina): Thanks so much for having us, super excited. This is Maya, our marketing director, and Rajiv and Ethan from engineering.

[01:05] Avery: Great. Quick housekeeping — Jordan's recording and Samir is running audio, we'll pull a few clips for social, and we'll send the edited draft back. Is that all good?

[01:40] Jordan (Redwood): Yep, we'll aim to get the first cut to you by next week.

[02:00] Maya (Lumina): Sounds perfect. We also have a couple of messaging points we'd like emphasized — patient privacy and low-latency triage support in urgent care.

[03:10] Avery: Awesome. Maybe to kick off, Sofia can you give us the short version — what problem were you trying to solve and why Redwood?

[03:45] Sofia: Sure. At Lumina we needed to automate patient intake notes and triage recommendations across clinics. We were seeing a ton of manual work and inconsistent summaries. We also had strict security and residency needs — PHI concerns, SOC 2 obligations.

[04:30] Rajiv (Lumina): From a tech perspective, before Redwood we had a mix of hosted endpoints and some self-hosted models but scaling was a mess. We needed consistent latency under 300ms 95th, and predictable cost. Redwood's dedicated offering gave us reserved capacity and the routing controls we needed.

[05:20] Avery: Nice. Can you share a specific metric — like latency, cost, or time saved?

[05:40] Ethan (Lumina): Yeah — for triage generation we've cut average turnaround from 45 seconds to about 800ms on our p95 after switching to Redwood Dedicated, and saved roughly 40% on token cost via caching and batching config suggestions.

[06:15] Maya: On the org side, we reduced manual intake reviews by about 60%, which freed nurses to focus on patient care and boosted satisfaction scores. That's obviously a big story for marketing.

[07:00] Avery: Love that. Were there any surprises during onboarding? Any bumps?

[07:30] Rajiv: A few. We underestimated the complexity of our deployment network — our VPC setup and some strict egress rules caused a delay. Also some model artifact naming differences caused the runtime to pick non-optimal kernels at first — small naming mismatch. But Redwood's SE worked with us to tune the compilation and kernel selection.

[08:20] Jordan: I remember that — we did a few bench runs and adjusted the kernel hints. The KV cache — or as some folks call it the K V cash in the transcript — was a big win once configured.

[08:55] Sofia: (laughs) Yes, KV cache was a bit of a revelation, honestly. Once the prefix caching was on, the repeat prompts in a session were nearly free.

[09:30] Avery: On the security front — what did you need from us?

[09:50] Sofia: We had questions around KMS integration, audit logs, and retention. Redwood provided a SOC 2 report and detailed logs; we also worked with their Private team for a customer-managed control plane in our cloud region, which helped with residency.

[10:40] Rajiv: The HSM/KMS integration was straightforward. We used our existing KMS key to encrypt payloads at rest, and Redwood supported the exchange quickly. There were some docs typos but overall good.

[11:20] Avery: Great to hear. For the podcast, Maya wanted a couple of soundbites on business impact. Maya, do you want to say the line you suggested earlier about reclaiming nursing time?

[11:42] Maya: Sure — "By automating intake triage with Redwood, we've reclaimed hundreds of nursing hours each month and improved patient throughput without sacrificing safety."

[12:10] Jordan: "That's a great quote — we'll flag it in the edit."

[12:35] Ethan: A technical soundbite — "The Redwood runtime's continuous batching and smart routing let us hit predictable p95 latency even during peak clinic hours."

[13:00] Avery: Perfect. Switching gears — any talk about models? You're using a mix of open models for clinical summarization and a custom fine-tuned model for triage, right?

[13:25] Rajiv: Exactly. We fine-tuned an open 7B for our triage rules and use a larger base model for free-form notes. Redwood's model catalog helped us compare performance quickly. We did raise costs vs accuracy tradeoffs and ended up quantizing some weights to reduce GPU memory.

[14:10] Sofia: The quantization recommendation from Redwood Optimize saved us a ton — reduced instance footprint so we could use a cheaper hardware tier without losing quality.

[14:45] Avery: Any hesitations about quality drift or hallucinations? How do you monitor?

[15:05] Ethan: We built a small evaluation harness on top of Redwood's rollouts and quality monitoring. We run prompt sets nightly and get regression alerts tied to example prompts, so we can rollback quickly if we see degradations.

[15:45] Maya: From marketing, we appreciate the eval dashboards because they give us confidence when we quote numbers externally.

[16:10] Jordan: Nice. For the podcast flow, we also want a short narrative about the pilot and ramp. Sofia, can you summarize timelines?

[16:30] Sofia: Pilot started January 2026 — two clinics, six weeks of iteration, then regional rollout in February. By end of February we were at 50 clinics and saw the metrics Ethan mentioned.

[17:05] Avery: That's a very tight ramp. Were any stakeholders surprised by the speed?

[17:25] Sofia: Execs were pleasantly surprised. The combination of Redwood Dedicated and the routing policies meant we didn't have to wait for infra projects. That was a selling point to leadership.

[18:00] Rajiv: One piece that was underestimated was data mapping for EHR integration — different clinics had slightly different field names, which made some prompts noisy. We standardized schemas and used a small normalization step pre-prompt which fixed the problem.

[18:45] Avery: Good practical tip. Okay, let's capture a few more quotes for the case study: maybe one on security and one on integration speed.

[19:05] Sofia: For security: "We were able to meet our data residency and SOC 2 requirements while still using modern model serving — that was crucial for legal clearance."

[19:35] Rajiv: For speed: "From pilot to 50 clinics in six weeks — we could not have done that without predictable dedicated capacity and the deployment tooling Redwood provided."

[20:05] Maya: Also, for creative: "The summary quality is now consistent, which makes it easier for clinicians to trust the model output."

[20:30] Avery: Excellent. A few lightning technical questions that some listeners might ask — any comments on cost controls, autoscaling and fallbacks?

[20:55] Ethan: We use reserved capacity for baseline throughput and burst to on-demand during spikes. We also have automatic fallback to a smaller model variant for non-critical paths and we route non-sensitive aggregation tasks to hosted endpoints to save cost.

[21:30] Avery: Were there conversations about on-prem or private deployment?

[21:50] Rajiv: We evaluated private on-prem but settled on VPC deployment with a customer-managed control plane, because it hit the mix of security and operational simplicity. On-prem would have been heavier operationally.

[22:25] Jordan: Quick note for the cut — there's a small laugh from Sofia at 08:55 that's charming; we should keep it.

[22:40] Maya: Also think about a 20-second clip about reclaimed nursing hours for LinkedIn.

[23:05] Avery: Great. Any concerns or unresolved items?

[23:25] Sofia: Just one — we want to make sure the patient-facing wording in the marketing piece is cleared by legal, so send us the final quotes.

[23:50] Avery: Absolutely. We'll send the quote approvals and a release form.

[24:15] Ethan: Small tech caveat — the first benchmark in our doc had a mislabelled column that made latency look better than it was; we fixed that before the rollout. Might be worth noting if anyone asks about numbers.

[24:55] Avery: Good transparency. For the case study draft, would Lumina prefer to see the draft before we write kerning on the final? (laughter) sorry, autocorrect, I mean 'before we finalize the copy'.

[25:20] Maya: Yes, we'd like to review. We also want our CISO on the approval chain for anything that mentions KMS.

[25:45] Jordan: We'll add a review step for CISO.

[26:10] Avery: Ok, let's do a quick run of the narrative arc for the episode: problem, pilot, results, technical learnings, and a closing call-to-action. Any additions?

[26:35] Sofia: Maybe an anecdote about a clinic nurse who said the summaries helped them catch a medication conflict earlier — human story is always good.

[27:05] Maya: We can send that anecdote as an approved quote.

[27:30] Avery: Nice. A few production notes: keep the episode to ~18 minutes; we'll probably cut most of the deep technical bits for the main episode and keep an extended engineer's cut for the blog. Jordan, thoughts?

[27:55] Jordan: Yep, 18 min main + extended 30-40 min tech deep-dive is a good plan. We'll prepare both edits.

[28:20] Samir (Audio): I'll clean up background noise at 15:10 where a siren came through.

[28:40] Avery: Great. Any last-minute promo asks from Lumina?

[29:00] Maya: We want a suggested tweet and LinkedIn post, and co-branded assets. Also please include the headshots and logo.

[29:30] Jordan: We'll include suggested social copy and some pull quotes.

[29:50] Sofia: One more technical question from Ethan — did Redwood's team see any model regressions after quantization?

[30:10] Avery: There were minor regressions on a few prompts during a test. Redwood Optimize recommended targeted re-tuning and a partial-quant approach — we can share the evaluation logs.

[30:40] Ethan: That's perfect — send the logs.

[30:55] Rajiv: We also appreciated the rollback policy — the A/B canary made us comfortable to push changes quickly.

[31:20] Avery: Good to hear. We're nearly at the end — any final quotes you want to record live?

[31:40] Sofia: Live quote: "Partnering with Redwood let us move from pilot to production faster than we imagined while keeping patient data safe."

[32:05] Maya: Live quote: "The time savings are real — clinicians are spending more time with patients, not on paperwork."

[32:30] Rajiv: Live technical quote: "Predictable p95 latency at scale was the single biggest enabler for productionizing our triage model."

[33:00] Avery: Those are awesome. We'll capture those as clean clips.

[33:20] Jordan: Recap of next steps: Jordan to send audio draft by 2026-03-25; Avery will send case study draft and release form; Lumina to return approvals and CISO sign-off by 2026-03-27.

[33:45] Sofia: Confirmed.

[34:00] Avery: Any other risks or follow-ups?

[34:20] Rajiv: We'll follow up on EHR schema normalization docs — Ethan will share a sanitized example.

[34:40] Ethan: Yep I'll drop that in the shared folder later today.

[35:00] Maya: We'll also schedule a cross-promo plan for the week of publishing.

[35:20] Jordan: Great. We'll pin a tentative publish window — aiming for the first week of April pending approvals.

[35:40] Avery: Perfect. Okay, thanks everyone. This was great. We'll send the edit and the release form and keep you posted.

[36:00] (brief off-mic chatter and goodbyes)

[41:00] End of recording.

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mishears ("K V cash" instead of KV cache), and mild punctuation issues from auto-transcription. References shared: case study draft (link to internal doc), audio draft (will be shared via file transfer).
